text:
Make a chat with a model twice as long, and its bill roughly triples. [curious] So why doesn't it just double?

Because the model keeps no memory between turns. So every turn, the app sends the whole chat again, from the top. Turn one sends a two-thousand-token system prompt and your first message. Turn two sends all of that again, plus the reply and your next message. That's five hundred fifty new tokens. Every turn resends the last one and adds a slice, so the requests climb like a staircase. By turn forty, one request is twenty-three thousand six hundred tokens.

You pay for every one of those bars. So the bill is the area under the staircase, plus the replies. Cut that area in two. The bottom is a rectangle: the system prompt, the same every turn. On top sits a triangle: the chat itself, sent again and again. Now double the turns. The rectangle just gets twice as long. But the triangle gets twice as long and twice as tall, so four of the old one fit inside.

On Sonnet, ten turns cost thirteen cents. Twenty, thirty-seven and a half. Forty, a dollar nineteen. That's two point eight times, then three point two. Eighty turns would be three and a half. The longer the chat, the more of the bill is triangle, so each doubling creeps toward four times.

Prompt caching goes after the triangle. You still send it all, but whatever you sent last turn is read back at a twentieth of the price. Only the new slice pays in full, so the staircase flattens. Forty turns drop from a dollar nineteen to twenty-six cents. So put whatever never changes first, where the cache can match it.

And when a chat runs long, start a fresh one. Eight five-turn chats cost forty-two cents. One forty-turn chat, a dollar nineteen. A chat grows by one slice a turn. Its bill grows by the whole chat.
